tip: 'Orang tua' = parents (literally 'old people'): 'orang tua saya' = my parents.
'Ada' isn't 'have' here – it marks that something is somewhere: 'kantor pos ada di sebelah kanan' = the post office is on the right. Indonesian normally drops 'is', but location keeps 'ada'.
'Jauh dari' = far from; 'dekat dengan' = near to.
'Naik' + vehicle = take/ride: 'naik bus' = take the bus.
'Di' + position word: 'di atas meja' = on (top of) the table.
Descriptions follow the noun and 'that' comes last: 'tas hitam itu' = bag-black-that. English order is reversed – 'itu' always closes the phrase.
The owner follows the thing owned: 'mobil saya' = car-my. No 's and no 'of' – just put the possessor right after the noun it belongs to.
'Jam' goes before the number for clock time: 'jam sembilan' = nine o'clock. Flip it to 'sembilan jam' and it means nine hours – the order decides which.
No do/does shuffle in questions: 'berapa lama' (how long) just sits where the answer would, keeping plain statement order: 'dari sini ke bandara berapa lama?'
'Ter-' + adjective = the most: 'terdekat' = the nearest, from 'dekat' (near).
'Kami' means 'we, not including you': 'kantor kami' = our office, but not yours. If the listener is part of the group, Indonesian switches to 'kita'.
Verbs never change for tense – 'sudah' does the work: 'sudah mengirim' = have already sent. Drop 'sudah' and the same sentence could be present or future.
'Jangan' = don't (command): 'jangan lupa!' = don't forget!
'Dia' is both 'he' and 'she' – Indonesian pronouns ignore gender. 'Dia sedang bekerja' could describe anyone; only context tells you who.
'Yang' links a noun to its description: 'orang yang duduk' = the person who is sitting.
'Yang' also links a noun to what someone did to it: 'baju yang kamu beli' = the shirt that you bought.
The verb after 'yang' can keep its own subject: 'yang dia masak' = that she cooks.
No verb for 'goes' here – 'yang ke' is enough: 'bus yang ke bandara' = the bus that goes to the airport.
'Daripada' is only for comparing; 'from' a place is plain 'dari'.
'Lebih suka' = prefer; 'daripada' introduces the option you like less: 'lebih suka teh daripada kopi' = prefer tea to coffee.
'Mana yang lebih' + adjective asks 'which one is more': 'mana yang lebih murah?' = which is cheaper?
'Paling' before an adjective makes 'the most': 'paling rajin' = the most diligent.
'Yang' here means 'the one': 'kamar ini yang paling murah' = this room is the one that's cheapest. Without 'yang' it's just 'this room is cheapest'.
'Mana' after a noun asks 'which': 'stasiun mana' = which station.
'Se-' + adjective means 'as ... as': 'setinggi ayah' = as tall as father.
'Tidak se-' + adjective = 'not as ... as': 'tidak sesulit' = not as hard as.
'Tolong' before a verb makes a polite request: 'tolong tutup pintu' = please close the door.
Doubling an adjective often makes a gentle adverb: 'pelan-pelan' = slowly.
'Dulu' tacked on at the end means 'first, before anything else': 'saya ambil uang dulu' = I'll get money first.
In requests the bare root is normal: 'tolong panggil', not 'tolong memanggil'.
